evidenceAudit.scope: Starting and adjusting insulin in adults with type 2 diabetes and people with type 1 diabetes in India: indications, basal insulin start and titration, adding prandial insulin, premixed insulin, targets, self-monitoring, hypoglycaemia treatment and sick-day rules, built on the ICMR Type 2 and Type 1 Diabetes STWs (July 2022) and the ADA Standards of Care 2025 section 9 for doses not in the ICMR workflows.
findings: Insulin for HbA1c above 10% added to oral agents, targets (HbA1c 7% or below; pre-meal 80–130 mg/dL; post-meal below 180 mg/dL), and monitoring checked against the ICMR Type 2 Diabetes STW (July 2022).

Total daily dose 0.25–1.0 U/kg, 40–50% basal and 50% bolus in 3 doses, hypoglycaemia with 3 teaspoons glucose, glucagon 1 mg SC/IM, 25% dextrose 1–2 mL/kg, sick-day extra regular insulin 10–15% of total daily dose every 6 hours and admission criteria checked against the ICMR Type 1 Diabetes STW (July 2022).

Basal start 0.1–0.2 U/kg/day, insulin when HbA1c above 10% or glucose 300 mg/dL or more, prandial start 4 units or 10% of basal at the largest meal, premixed twice daily option, overbasalisation signs and glucagon for everyone on insulin checked against the ADA Standards of Care 2025 section 9.

Self-titration of basal insulin by 2 units every 3 days, overbasalisation above 0.5 U/kg, prandial start of 4 units or 10% of basal with basal reduction by 4 units or 10% when HbA1c is below 8%, and prandial reduction of 10–20% for hypoglycaemia checked against the ADA Overcoming Therapeutic Inertia titration guide (2024 Standards).
unverifiedSections: The ICMR Type 2 STW gives no insulin doses or titration; these come from ADA 2025.
The 2-units-every-3-days titration rule and the overbasalisation threshold (above 0.5 U/kg) are from the ADA Overcoming Therapeutic Inertia guide based on the 2024 Standards.
Insulin storage and injection-technique advice is general practice.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Many Indians with type 2 diabetes need insulin, often late because of fear and cost. The ICMR workflow adds basal insulin when HbA1c is above 10% despite oral drugs; ADA 2025 also advises insulin at any stage for symptomatic hyperglycaemia, catabolic features or glucose 300 mg/dL or more. Basal insulin (NPH or glargine) is started at bedtime at 0.1–0.2 U/kg and titrated to fasting glucose; prandial insulin or twice-daily premixed insulin is added when fasting glucose is controlled but HbA1c remains high. Type 1 diabetes needs basal-bolus insulin from diagnosis. Every person on insulin needs self-monitoring, hypoglycaemia education, glucagon where available and sick-day rules. A practical rule makes self-titration safe: adjust basal insulin by 2 units every 3 days towards the fasting target, and stop escalating once the dose passes about 0.5 units/kg without control.
keyMechanisms: Type 2 diabetes progresses with declining beta-cell function, so many eventually need insulin.
Basal insulin suppresses hepatic glucose output overnight and between meals.
Prandial insulin covers meal-related glucose rises.
Too much basal insulin (overbasalisation) causes hypoglycaemia and wide glucose swings.

symptoms: Polyuria, thirst, weight loss despite treatment
Blurred vision, recurrent infections (genital candidiasis, skin)
Nocturnal sweating or morning headache (nocturnal hypoglycaemia)
physicalSigns: Low BMI or rapid weight loss despite treatment (insulin deficiency)
redFlags: Glucose 300 mg/dL or more or HbA1c above 10% with symptoms: start insulin (ADA 2025)
Ketones with glucose above 250 mg/dL: sick-day rules or admit (ICMR T1DM)
Vomiting, poor urine output, rising ketones: admit (ICMR T1DM)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Lean adult whose oral drugs fail within months; GAD antibodies positive and C-peptide low — needs insulin early.
Common in parts of India: young, lean, recurrent abdominal pain and steatorrhoea; pancreatic calcification on X-ray or ultrasound; needs insulin and enzymes.
Afternoon and evening glucose rise on prednisolone or dexamethasone with near-normal fasting values; morning NPH or prandial insulin fits the pattern.
Weight loss, ketones and low C-peptide; needs basal-bolus insulin from diagnosis, never oral drugs alone.

differentials.condition: Overbasalisation rather than true insulin resistance
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Basal dose above 0.5 U/kg, bedtime-to-morning glucose fall of 50 mg/dL or more, or hypoglycaemia; add prandial insulin instead of more basal.
High fasting glucose explained by a 2–3 am check: low at night (too much evening insulin) or normal at night with a dawn rise.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Symptoms, catabolic features, HbA1c above 10% or glucose 300 mg/dL or more.
Bedtime-to-morning glucose fall 50 mg/dL or more, hypoglycaemia or high variability.
HbA1c 7% or below; pre-meal 80–130 mg/dL; post-meal below 180 mg/dL.

clinicalManagement.title: Start basal insulin
actions: Continue metformin and other oral agents unless contraindicated (ADA 2025).
Teach injection, SMBG and hypoglycaemia treatment; prescribe glucagon where available (ADA 2025).

clinicalManagement.title: Titrate
actions: Patient adjusts basal dose by 2 units every 3 days until fasting glucose reaches target (80–130 mg/dL) (ADA guide; ICMR T2DM).
Any hypoglycaemia: find the cause and lower the dose (ADA guide).
Basal above 0.5 U/kg without control, or bedtime-to-morning fall 50 mg/dL or more: stop escalating basal (ADA 2025; ADA guide).

clinicalManagement.title: Intensify
clinicalManagement.timeframe: When fasting controlled but HbA1c high
actions: Add prandial insulin 4 units or 10% of basal before the largest meal (ADA 2025).
Or switch to premixed insulin twice daily (ADA 2025).

clinicalManagement.title: Adjust prandial insulin
actions: Titrate prandial dose by post-meal readings (no step size stated in the opened sources); if HbA1c below 8% when adding prandial, reduce basal by 4 units or 10% (ADA guide).
Hypoglycaemia on prandial insulin: reduce that dose by 10–20% (ADA guide).

clinicalManagement.title: Type 1 diabetes
actions: Total daily dose 0.25–1.0 U/kg: 40–50% basal, 50% bolus split before 3 meals (ICMR T1DM).
Sick days: extra regular insulin 10–15% of total daily dose every 6 hours; admit if not settling (ICMR T1DM).

clinicalManagement.title: Hypoglycaemia
actions: Below 70 mg/dL: 3 teaspoons glucose or sugar (ICMR T1DM).
Severe: glucagon 1 mg SC/IM, then 25% dextrose 1–2 mL/kg IV in hospital (ICMR T1DM).

vignette.text: Mrs S, a 54-year-old school teacher from Chennai with type 2 diabetes for 11 years, takes metformin 1 g twice daily and glimepiride 4 mg daily. She has lost 4 kg in 3 months, has nocturia, and her HbA1c is 10.8% with fasting glucose 238 mg/dL. Weight is 68 kg, eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73 m². She is afraid that insulin means 'the last stage' and that injections will hurt.

guidedApproach.title: Why most people with type 2 diabetes eventually need insulin
guidedApproach.guidance: Type 2 diabetes is a progressive loss of beta-cell function on a background of insulin resistance. Oral drugs and lifestyle changes work while enough beta-cell function remains, but over a decade many people — and in India, often earlier and at a lower body weight — no longer make enough insulin. Weight loss, rising glucose despite good adherence and catabolic features are signs of insulin deficiency, not of poor effort. Basal insulin replaces the background insulin that suppresses glucose production from the liver overnight and between meals, which is why it lowers fasting glucose so effectively. Prandial insulin covers the glucose rise after meals. Explaining this removes the stigma that insulin is a punishment or the 'last stage'.

guidedApproach.title: Recognising when insulin is needed — and when it is too much
guidedApproach.prompt: Which features tell you to start, and which tell you to stop escalating?
guidedApproach.guidance: Start insulin when HbA1c is above 10%, glucose is 300 mg/dL or more, or the patient has symptoms such as weight loss, polyuria and thirst (ADA 2025; ICMR uses HbA1c above 10%). Look for type 1 diabetes or LADA in lean adults whose oral drugs fail early, and for fibrocalculous pancreatic diabetes in young lean patients with abdominal pain. Once on insulin, watch for overbasalisation: a basal dose above about 0.5 units/kg, a fall of 50 mg/dL or more from bedtime to morning, hypoglycaemia, or widely swinging readings. These mean the patient needs prandial cover, not more basal insulin. Night sweats, nightmares and morning headaches suggest nocturnal hypoglycaemia; a check between midnight and 2 am confirms it.

guidedApproach.title: Monitoring that makes titration safe
guidedApproach.prompt: What does the patient need to measure?
guidedApproach.guidance: Self-monitoring of blood glucose is what makes insulin safe. During basal titration the key reading is the fasting glucose each morning; when prandial insulin is added, readings 2 hours after meals guide those doses. People with type 1 diabetes test before each meal and at bedtime, with an occasional check between midnight and 2 am. HbA1c every 3 months shows whether the overall plan is working. Check ketones when glucose is above 250 mg/dL during illness. Annual creatinine and eGFR matter because insulin needs fall as kidney function declines, and the injection sites should be examined at every visit for lipohypertrophy, which causes erratic absorption.

guidedApproach.title: A stepwise insulin plan
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you start, titrate and intensify?
guidedApproach.guidance: Keep metformin and other non-insulin drugs unless contraindicated, and reduce or stop the sulfonylurea when prandial insulin is added. Start basal insulin at 0.1–0.2 units/kg at bedtime — NPH is cheaper, glargine causes less nocturnal hypoglycaemia. Teach the patient to raise the dose by 2 units every 3 days until fasting glucose reaches 80–130 mg/dL, and to lower it after any hypoglycaemia. When fasting glucose is at target but HbA1c is still high, or the basal dose exceeds about 0.5 units/kg, add 4 units (or 10% of the basal dose) of prandial insulin before the largest meal, or switch to premixed insulin twice daily. Every patient on insulin needs a hypoglycaemia plan: 3 teaspoons of glucose for mild episodes, glucagon 1 mg for severe ones, and sick-day rules.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 54-year-old school teacher with type 2 diabetes for 11 years takes metformin 1 g twice daily and glimepiride 4 mg daily with good adherence. HbA1c is 10.8%, fasting glucose 238 mg/dL, and she has lost 4 kg in 3 months with nocturia. Weight is 68 kg and eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73 m².
boardQuestions.question: What is the best next step?

options.text: Add a third oral drug and review in 6 months
options.explanation: Weight loss with HbA1c above 10% indicates insulin deficiency; insulin is recommended (ADA 2025; ICMR).

options.text: Start basal insulin about 7–14 units at bedtime and continue metformin
options.explanation: Correct. 0.1–0.2 U/kg for 68 kg is about 7–14 units; keep metformin (ADA 2025).

options.text: Stop all oral drugs and start basal-bolus insulin 1 U/kg/day
options.explanation: Too much, too fast: basal insulin is started first and metformin continued.

options.text: Start premixed insulin 30 units twice daily
options.explanation: An unnecessarily high starting dose with high hypoglycaemia risk.
Higher sulfonylurea doses add little and raise hypoglycaemia risk when beta-cell function is failing.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Recognise the indication for insulin and choose a safe starting dose.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Start basal 0.1–0.2 U/kg at bedtime; keep metformin.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 60-year-old man on glargine has titrated to 52 units daily (weight 80 kg). Fasting glucose is 110–125 mg/dL, but HbA1c is 8.9% and he has had two episodes of hypoglycaemia at 3 am. Bedtime glucose is around 220 mg/dL.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate change?

options.explanation: He is overbasalised; more basal insulin increases nocturnal hypoglycaemia.

options.text: Switch glargine to NPH at the same dose
options.explanation: NPH increases nocturnal hypoglycaemia risk and does not address post-meal glucose.
A sulfonylurea adds hypoglycaemia risk and does not target the problem.

options.text: Reduce glargine and add prandial insulin before the largest meal
options.explanation: Correct. Basal above 0.5 U/kg (52 units for 80 kg = 0.65 U/kg), a large bedtime-to-morning fall and nocturnal hypoglycaemia signal overbasalisation; add prandial cover (ADA guide).

options.text: No change because fasting glucose is at target
options.explanation: HbA1c above goal with nocturnal hypoglycaemia needs a change.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Recognise overbasalisation and intensify with prandial insulin.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Basal above 0.5 U/kg with hypoglycaemia or large overnight fall: add prandial insulin, not more basal.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 19-year-old college student with type 1 diabetes on basal-bolus insulin (total 48 units a day) phones the clinic. He has fever and has vomited twice since morning. His glucose is 310 mg/dL and urine ketones are moderate. He can still drink fluids and asks whether he should skip insulin because he cannot eat.
boardQuestions.question: What is the correct advice?

options.text: Stop all insulin until he can eat
options.explanation: Stopping insulin precipitates diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA); insulin is never stopped on sick days (ICMR T1DM).

options.text: Continue usual insulin and add regular insulin 10–15% of the total daily dose every 6 hours, with fluids and glucose checks; come in if vomiting persists or ketones rise
options.explanation: Correct. These are the ICMR T1DM sick-day rules with admission criteria.

options.text: Take only basal insulin and no extra
options.explanation: Basal alone is not enough; he needs extra insulin to clear the ketones.
Illness raises insulin needs; halving doses risks DKA.
His glucose is already high; he needs insulin, fluids and close monitoring, not extra glucose.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Apply sick-day rules in type 1 diabetes.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Never stop insulin when ill; give extra 10–15% of TDD every 6 hours and admit if not settling.

patientEducation: Recognise and treat hypoglycaemia; carry sugar.
Never stop insulin when ill; check ketones.
lifestyleAndDiet: Regular meals matched to insulin; carbohydrate awareness; exercise planning.
dischargeCriteria: Able to inject and test glucose
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Phone or clinic review within 1–2 weeks of starting; HbA1c every 3 months until stable (ICMR T1DM; ICMR T2DM when uncontrolled).
